text:
Help me write a public comment. I run a charter fishing boat out of our harbor, and the state fish and wildlife commission is taking comment on cutting the daily summer flounder limit from 4 fish per angler to 2.

Facts:
- I've run my boat for 22 years. I take out about 160 trips a season at $900 a trip for up to 6 people.
- There are 11 charter boats in our harbor.
- In a survey our charter association ran, 41 of 70 past customers said they would book fewer trips if the limit drops to 2. 12 said they'd book the same number.
- The commission staff's report says the flounder stock is at 78% of its target and recommends the cut for 3 years.
- Charter boats land about 9% of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%.
- The last time the limit was cut, in 2016, my bookings dropped from 170 trips to 138 the next season and came back to 155 two years later.

I want to say this limit will put every charter boat in our harbor out of business. I get two minutes at the microphone.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the comment says.

1. **What do you want the commission to do instead?** You could ask them to keep 4, go to 3, set a separate charter limit (charters land 9% and private boats land 80%), shorten the cut to fewer than 3 years, or review it after a year. Commissioners are more likely to act on a specific alternative than on a plain "no."

2. **How many trips a season do you need to break even?** I'm asking because of the "out of business" line. Your own 2016 numbers show you lost 32 trips and stayed open. If you say "every boat will close," a commissioner will probably point to that. If you can say "below X trips I can't cover fuel, insurance and the boat payment," we can make a strong claim that holds up.

3. **Did any boats in your harbor close or sell after the 2016 cut?** Or are any of the 11 struggling now? A real example would carry a lot of weight.

4. **What did the 2016 cut go from and to?** Was it about the same size as 4 to 2? That tells us whether 2016 is a fair guide to next season.

5. **Did the survey ask how many fewer trips people would book?** Or just whether they'd book fewer? Even rough numbers would help.

If you don't know some of these, just say so. I'll write around them and won't guess.

1. We'd take a 3-fish limit or a shorter season instead of 2. Either one.

2. I don't know my break-even number off hand.

3. None that I know of closed after 2016. But two other captains here have told me they'd sell if bookings drop like they did in 2016. I can't say how many boats would actually close. I only know my own books. I still want to say every boat will go under, but if that's past the facts, make it as strong as you can without saying something false.

4. I don't know what the 2016 cut went from and to.

5. I don't know. I think it just asked if they'd book fewer.

I wrote it without "every boat will go under." The 2016 numbers are the problem: you lost 32 trips, nobody in your harbor closed, and you only know your own books. If you say every boat will close, a commissioner can point that out and the rest of your comment loses force. The strongest true version is that 2016 hurt and you never fully recovered, a 3-year cut is worse, and two captains have told you they'd sell. That's specific, it's real, and they can't knock it down.

<final_document>
Good evening, Commissioners. My name is [NAME]. I've run a charter boat out of [HARBOR] for 22 years. I'm one of 11 charter boats there.

I'm not here to tell you the stock is fine. Your staff says flounder are at 78% of target, and I want them around for the next 22 years too. I'm asking you to get there without cutting the limit to two.

I've been through this before. When the limit was cut in 2016, my bookings fell from 170 trips to 138 the next season. At today's price, that's nearly $29,000 gone in one year. Two years later I'd only climbed back to 155. I never got all the way back.

That was one cut. This one runs three years. Our charter association asked 70 past customers what they'd do at two fish. Forty-one said they'd book fewer trips. Only 12 said they'd book the same.

Two captains in my harbor have already told me that if bookings drop like they did in 2016, they'll sell. Three lean years in a row is more than a lot of us can carry.

Charter boats land about 9% of this state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%. For a private angler, two fish means a smaller day. For us, it decides whether the customer books at all.

So I'm asking for either of two things: a three-fish limit, or a shorter season. Either one protects the stock without putting charter boats through three years like the one I had after 2016.

Thank you.
</final_document>

Some notes:

- **Length:** It's about 260 words, which takes roughly two minutes at a steady pace. Read it out loud with a timer once. If you run long, cut the 9%/80% paragraph first.
- **The dollar figure:** "Nearly $29,000" is 32 trips at your current $900 rate. That's why it says "at today's price." If your 2016 rate was different, you can use the real 2016 figure or keep the line as written.
- **The survey:** Be ready if someone asks about it. It came from your association, and it only asked whether people would book fewer trips, not how many fewer. Saying that openly will make you more credible.
- **Before the meeting:** Try to work out roughly how many trips a season you need to cover your costs. If a commissioner asks "would you actually go under?", that number is the best answer you could give.
